Her chair scraped backward as she stood. “You think I copied this?” she asked. “I found it in the library database and cited it in my notes. Check the document history.” The professor began typing, but Mara could hear the clock ticking above them, each click striking like a hammer.

By the time the records appeared, her draft had been saved weeks before the article was uploaded. Professor Bell’s face changed. Mara gathered her papers with stiff, deliberate movements. She did not apologize when he offered to remove the accusation. She simply looked at the copied article and said, “Find out who stole from whom.”

Mara stood behind the chain-link fence as the excavator lifted its steel arm toward the house. The yellow machine had already crushed the porch steps, the same steps where her father used to sit and peel apples with a pocketknife. She gripped the fence until its wires pressed crescents into her palms. “You said Friday,” she called to the foreman. “Today is Thursday.” He glanced at his clipboard and told her the schedule had changed. Mara laughed once, sharply. “Of course it did.” Then she pulled out her phone and began photographing every window, every crack in the brick, every mark on the doorframe. When the bucket swung forward, she shouted the house’s address as if forcing the workers to hear the name before it vanished.

By the time Elise arrived at the bakery, her replacement had already learned where the cinnamon rolls were stored.

The girl—Tessa, according to the name tag—stood behind the counter wearing Elise’s old green apron. The manager had removed Elise’s name and pinned on the new one, leaving two tiny holes in the fabric.

“Show her the morning routine,” the manager ordered.

Elise placed both hands on the counter. Flour dust drifted between her fingers. “She’s wearing my apron.”

“It’s company property.”

“So is the oven. You don’t see me taking that home.”

The manager’s lips tightened, but Tessa looked down at the pastry case. She seemed barely twenty, with a nervous habit of rubbing her thumb along the edge of her notebook.

Elise exhaled through her nose and began.

She demonstrated how to judge dough by touch, how to listen for the change in the mixer’s rhythm, and how to hide the burnt trays before the manager came downstairs. When Tessa reached for a pan without a cloth, Elise caught her wrist.

“Unless you want to spend your first week with bandages, use this.”

“Right. Sorry.”

“Stop apologizing and pay attention.”

The words echoed through the empty kitchen. Tessa flinched. Elise saw it, then turned toward the sink and gripped its metal rim until the trembling in her hands settled.

After closing, Tessa found her near the back door.

“I heard they’re cutting your position because the new owners want younger staff,” she said quietly. “I’m sorry.”

Elise stared at the ovens glowing behind her. Twelve years of early mornings, burned fingertips, birthday cakes, wedding cakes, and unsold bread sat inside those walls.

“Don’t be sorry,” she said. “Just remember who taught you everything they’ll pretend you already knew.”

She untied the green apron, folded it into a square, and placed it on the manager’s desk. Then she left through the back door, letting it slam hard enough to rattle the bottles on the shelves.

Mara stood outside the apartment building, staring at the dented mailbox where her landlord had shoved another notice. Her thumb moved across her phone.

**You can’t keep charging me for repairs you never made. I’m done being treated like a walking wallet. Fix the heater by Friday, or I’ll make sure everyone in this building knows exactly how you operate.**

She hit send without looking at the name.

A moment later, three dots appeared.

**Hi, Mara. This is Daniel from accounting. Should I still bring the dessert to your mother’s birthday dinner?**

She froze. The phone nearly slipped from her hand. Then she looked at the recipient: Daniel, her younger brother.

From the open window above, the landlord called, “You have a problem with the rent?”

Mara shoved the phone into her coat pocket. “Not anymore,” she said, though her jaw remained clenched. She marched up the stairs, each footstep striking the concrete like a hammer.

At the second-floor landing, her phone buzzed again.

**Also, what does ‘walking wallet’ mean?**

She stopped, closed her eyes, and pressed two fingers against her forehead.

“Nothing,” she muttered. “It means absolutely nothing.”

Then she turned around and marched back toward the mailbox.

I recognized my painting on the man’s back before I recognized the man himself.

We were standing in line at the train station, surrounded by wet coats and the metallic shriek of arriving cars. The tattoo ran from his shoulder blade to his spine: my red-eyed saint, my brushstrokes, even the tiny white scar I had painted across the cheek.

I stepped forward.

“Excuse me,” I said.

He turned halfway, glancing over his shoulder.

“Where did you get that?”

He smiled. “A tattoo artist in Brixton. Found the design online.”

“Who gave you permission?”

His smile faded. I could hear the paper in my hand crumpling as my fingers folded tighter around it.

“It’s just a tattoo.”

I laughed once, without humor. “It was six months of my life.”

The train doors opened. People pushed past us, but I stayed rooted to the platform, staring at the stolen image moving beneath his skin. When he walked away, I pulled out my phone and began photographing him from behind.

Jonah was signing posters at a gallery opening when the woman in the green coat lifted her sleeve.

His painting stared back at him from her shoulder.

The original hung twenty feet away: a black ocean beneath a yellow sky, with one small figure standing ankle-deep in the surf. Jonah had painted it during the winter his brother disappeared. He had sold the canvas once, then bought it back because he could not bear to lose it.

Now the same figure rose and fell with the woman’s breathing.

“You’re the artist, right?” she asked. “I had this done because your painting saved me.”

Jonah looked from the tattoo to the canvas. The brushwork was exact—the thin white slash of foam, the uneven horizon, even the tiny mistake where his wrist had slipped near the figure’s head.

“Who gave you permission?” he said.

Her smile faded. “I thought you’d be flattered.”

The pen in his hand cracked. Black ink spilled across his fingers and dripped onto the signing table. Around them, conversations thinned into silence.

Jonah reached for the photograph he had been signing and turned it facedown.

“You took something I made when I was barely standing,” he said, his voice low and level. “You don’t get to decide what that means to me.”

The woman pulled her sleeve down. Jonah stepped away from the table, leaving the posters unsigned and the gallery lights glaring against the wet ink on his hands.

When Professor Vale placed the essay on the desk, Mara stared at the red circle around her name. “This passage matches a website,” he said. “You’ll receive a failing grade unless you explain yourself.”

Mara’s fingers tightened around the edge of the paper until it creased. “I wrote it,” she said, each word clipped short. “You didn’t even ask me where I found the sources.”

The professor opened his laptop and turned it toward her. The highlighted paragraph belonged to an obscure article she had never seen. Mara leaned closer, her pulse thudding in her ears. Then she noticed the date beneath the article: it had been published three days after she submitted her essay.

She pushed the paper back across the desk. “Check the submission record. Check the library database. Check anything you want—but don’t call me a cheat because you skipped the evidence.”

Mr. Vale found the package on his desk just after the final bell. It was wrapped in silver paper, with a note tucked beneath the ribbon: *For the teacher who kept me from quitting.* He tore it open and stared at the antique fountain pen inside—the very pen stolen from his desk twenty years earlier by Daniel Ortiz, the student who had denied it while the whole class watched. Mr. Vale’s fingers tightened around the box until the cardboard bent. When Daniel appeared in the doorway, smiling nervously, Mr. Vale set the pen down with careful precision. “You kept it all these years?” he asked. “I did,” Daniel said. “It reminded me that you believed I could become someone better.” Mr. Vale looked at the gleaming pen, then at the young man’s hopeful face. His jaw worked once. “You could have returned it sooner.” “I know.” Silence pressed between them. At last, Mr. Vale pushed the box back across the desk. “Then start by telling me the whole story.”

Mara bought the battered cookbook for two dollars because its pages were crowded with handwritten notes. At home, she dropped it onto the kitchen table and noticed an envelope tucked beneath the binding.

Her thumb tore it open. The letter inside was dated twenty years earlier.

*I know what you did to my sister. Everyone will learn the truth.*

Mara read the sentence twice. Then she looked toward the apartment next door, where her father had lived until last winter. His name appeared at the bottom of the page.

The cookbook snapped shut beneath her palms. She shoved it across the table so hard that a mug toppled and burst against the floor.

“No,” she said, though no one was there to hear her.

She picked up the letter again, smoothing the creases with fingers that would not stay still. By the time she reached for her phone, the paper had torn through the middle.

When the oak crashed through Maya’s fence, she stood on the porch with both hands locked around the railing. Splintered boards lay across her flower beds, and one thick branch had crushed the mailbox flat. Her neighbor appeared at the property line, still holding a rake. “It was leaning toward your yard,” he said. Maya turned slowly, her jaw tight. “Yes,” she replied. “That tends to matter when it falls.” She marched outside, picked up the broken mailbox, and carried it to his doorstep without another word.

Jonah was signing prints at a convention when a woman approached with his portrait tattooed across her shoulder. At first, he admired the precision. Then he noticed the missing scar above the subject’s eyebrow, the altered shadow beneath the chin, and the signature copied beneath the image. His pen snapped between his fingers. “This is not a tribute,” he said. The woman smiled and explained that a popular tattooist had sold the design as part of a collection. Jonah placed both palms flat on the table, keeping them there while the muscles in his jaw tightened. Around him, conversations thinned into silence. He asked for the tattooist’s name, wrote it on the back of a receipt, and drew a dark line beneath it. By the time the woman walked away, Jonah had removed every print from his display and replaced them with a handwritten sign: **ASK THE ARTIST FIRST.**

Mara found the photograph at 6:14 in the morning, while the kettle shrieked behind her. A stranger’s forearm filled the screen: her blue heron mural, every feather and crooked crescent moon copied exactly, now stretched across someone’s skin.

She set the phone down with such force that the mug beside it jumped.

For three years, Mara had painted that wall behind the old train station. She had mixed the colors herself, climbed the scaffolding herself, and spent two freezing nights correcting the heron’s left wing. The image belonged to a neighborhood, perhaps—but the design belonged to her.

She clicked through the tattoo studio’s page. There it was again, posted beneath the caption: *One of my favorite pieces yet.*

Mara’s fingers hovered over the keyboard. She typed, deleted, typed again.

“Did you ask the artist?”

The reply came minutes later.

“Art is meant to be shared.”

Mara stared at those four words until her jaw ached. Then she walked to the train station, carrying a ladder and three cans of paint. By noon, a white rectangle covered the copied heron’s face. Across it, in careful black letters, she wrote:

**ASK FIRST.**

By noon, the gallery walls were crowded with visitors, and Julian had almost convinced himself the opening was going well. Then he noticed the woman near the sculpture garden. His painted koi fish—his signature piece, copied from years of studying movement in water—curved across her neck in bright red and silver.

He crossed the room without greeting anyone.

“Who tattooed that?”

The woman blinked. “A studio downtown.”

“Did they ask permission?”

“Permission for what?”

Julian stopped in front of her. His hands opened and closed at his sides. Behind him, someone praised the painting that had made the tattoo possible. The sound scraped against him.

“That image is mine,” he said.

The woman glanced from the tattoo to the canvas. “I didn’t know.”

Julian turned toward the gallery owner. “You did.”

The owner’s smile vanished. “We sold reproduction rights for the exhibition brochure.”

“Not the tattoo.”

“No one can own a koi fish.”

Julian grabbed the brochure from the display table and folded it once, twice, until the glossy paper split down the middle. “Not a koi fish,” he said. “That composition. Those scales. That wound above the eye.”

The woman stepped away from him. Julian noticed and forced his hands into his coat pockets. He took out his phone, photographed the tattoo, and began listing every person who had entered his studio during the past year. Around him, the opening continued, glasses chiming beneath the bright gallery lights.
